physical_builder_candidate: LIMMCO / Long Island Musical Merchandise Co.
evidence_summary: Tone Machines identifies LIMMCO as a Hicksville New York distribution and wholesale company and describes Bob Seidman as a central connection among Applied, Nomad, Kimberly, UMI, Guild, Goya and related brands. A 1968 Billboard/NAMM listing independently places Limmco, Inc. among music-industry exhibitors.

physical_builder_candidate: LIMMCO initial build; later third parties
evidence_summary: Bob Seidman account reported by Tone Machines says Kimberly initially was made in the LIMMCO warehouse, then outside production was hired because in-house manufacture consumed too many resources. A May 1967 Music Trades advertisement is cited as a New Improved Circuit Design transition marker, but the surviving online source does not independently identify the intermediate factory by name.

model_or_family: Buzz Box and Volume Expander v2
evidence_summary: Effects Database explicitly lists a Kimberly Fuzz Box and Volume Expander v1 by LIMMCO and v2 by Applied. Tone Machines independently places Applied as the likely interim builder between LIMMCO and later UMI production, while noting this remains a reconstruction rather than a fully primary-source-proven factory contract.

model_or_family: Buzz Box and Volume Expander later state
evidence_summary: Effects Database relates Apollo No. 843 and Conrad Buzz Box & Volume Expander as UMI products derived from the Kimberly line. Tone Machines reports that UMI later produced the Kimberly-derived pedals through the end of the run. The exact handoff date remains open.

Tone Machines states the Nomad Banshee Fuzz was made by Applied Audio and distributed by LIMMCO, while also noting that manufacturing dates remain unknown. Nomad therefore supplies a clear example of a LIMMCO house brand crossing into a specific third-party factory relationship.

Tone Machines states the Nomad Rogue Fuzz was made by Applied Audio and followed the Banshee Fuzz, with an additional gain stage. The production date remains unresolved, so the model should not be used as a firm chronological anchor without further period evidence.

Effects Database and Tone Machines describe the rare Nomad Super Fuzz as an apparent OEM version of the early germanium Mosrite Fuzzrite circuit, but neither source establishes a direct Mosrite-Nomad transaction or an Applied build. The product therefore remains isolated from the later Applied Nomad family.

Effects Database catalogs a Nomad Tone Booster as Nomad by UMI. This supports a UMI relationship for this specific product state, but does not justify assigning the wider Nomad brand to UMI manufacture.

Tone Machines places Gracin's Fubar in the East Coast Fuzz family, but current evidence does not identify a factory. This record must remain separate from UMI's documented amplifier relationship with Gracin's Music and from Foxx-made Gracin's & Towne effects.

Effects Database explicitly identifies the Gracin's & Towne Wa & Volume as made by Foxx/fOXX. This is a concrete cross-supplier example under the Gracin's name and blocks any attempt to infer one factory from the label alone.

Tone Machines presents the Goya Panther Box as an Applied Audio product and ties the Goya relationship to Applied-era manufacturing. The chronology and exact contract dates remain incomplete, so the record is retained as research-validated rather than public-lineage promotion.

Tone Machines reports that Bob Seidman was an early U.S. intermediary in developing a U.S.-Japan musical-instrument business relationship that contributed to the Japanese import boom. This is useful network context but is not model-specific factory evidence for every LIMMCO brand or effect.
